performers: Skidmore College Orchestra; cellist and conductor uncredited
question: How does the cello connect forceful gestures with more sustained phrases?
intro: Musopen credits the Skidmore College Orchestra but does not name this recording’s cellist or conductor. The complete finale is heard here; only a shared passage is aligned with Harrison and Elgar’s heavily abridged acoustic version.

sections.label: Opening gestures
sections.mNote: measured listening spans, not a score-aligned formal map

sections.label: Early moving span
sections.mNote: shared passage with the acoustic version begins in this region

cues.title: The complete finale
cues.text: Listen to the contrast between the opening’s assertive gestures and its quieter spaces. This recording contains the full finale: its length should not be compared directly with an acoustic version that cuts substantial material.
cues.evidence: The report measures 693.7 seconds and shows an early relative-level rise around 0:05 followed by quieter windows around 0:20–0:25 and 0:45–0:55. The source identifies movement IV. https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Edward_Elgar_-_cello_concerto_in_e_minor,_op._85_-_iv._allegro.ogg

cues.title: Motion after the pauses
cues.text: Across this early moving stretch, attend to the cello’s articulation and the space between short figures. Compare the same material in Harrison’s acoustic record, rather than the total lengths of two differently cut versions.
cues.evidence: Detected attacks increase around 1:20–1:35 after sparse windows around 0:45–1:15. The comparison separately aligns 85–124 seconds here with 710–745 seconds in Harrison’s supplied whole-concerto stream; it is provisional, not bar alignment.

cues.title: Harrison was not the premiere soloist
cues.text: Felix Salmond played the concerto’s premiere on 27 October 1919, with Elgar conducting. Harrison’s early recordings belong to the work’s subsequent history, not to that first performance.
cues.evidence: The concerto’s history identifies Salmond and the premiere date, distinguishing him from Harrison in the recording account. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cello_Concerto_(Elgar)

cues.title: Two different Harrison recordings
cues.text: Harrison and Elgar made an abridged acoustic version before their first complete recording in 1928. The comparison uses the earlier version: a composer conducting his own work does not make every recorded cut part of the published score.
cues.evidence: The recording account distinguishes the acoustic abridgement from the complete 1928 Harrison–Elgar recording. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cello_Concerto_(Elgar)

cues.title: A stronger middle stretch
cues.text: The middle portion gathers into a stronger span, then retreats again. Follow the shape over several phrases rather than assuming that every rise starts a new section.
cues.evidence: The report identifies a boundary at 5:54, elevated relative level around 5:55–6:10 and a fall by 6:20. No score event or individual instrument is assigned to the boundary.

cues.title: Credit without a guessed soloist
cues.text: The source credits the Skidmore College Orchestra and Musopen, but does not name the cellist or conductor. Those omissions remain visible here; an institutional recording credit is not enough to identify an individual player.
cues.evidence: The Commons description names Skidmore College Orchestra, attributes the public-domain release to Musopen and provides no individual session personnel or date. https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?title=File:Edward_Elgar_-_cello_concerto_in_e_minor,_op._85_-_iv._allegro.ogg&action=raw

cues.title: More than one crest
cues.text: The late stretch alternates stronger gestures with withdrawals. Compare the space left after each swell: a retreat can prolong a phrase’s effect rather than simply undoing its growth.
cues.evidence: The strongest five-second windows include 9:00, 9:20 and 9:35, separated by lower relative levels around 9:05–9:15 and 9:25. This describes the recording’s contour, not a continuous crescendo.

cues.title: Quiet before the final drive
cues.text: Stay with the quieter sound late in the movement rather than anticipating the ending. The final resurgence gains force from the time spent withholding it.
cues.evidence: The report shows quiet windows around 10:40 and 11:00–11:10, followed by a rise from 11:15 through 11:30. The note does not claim the precise start of the final theme.

composer.epithet: A Worcester violinist who made orchestral variations into portraits of friends and the concerto into an argument with memory.
facts: Largely self-taught; violin, organ, orchestral playing and his father’s Worcester music shop
Bandmaster, Worcester County Asylum, Powick, 1879–84 · organist, St George’s Catholic Church, 1885–89 · Master of the King’s Musick, 1924–34
Two completed symphonies; violin and cello concertos; choral works; chamber music; five completed Pomp and Circumstance marches
composer.background:
Elgar learned the orchestra from inside it. His father William kept a music shop in Worcester, tuned pianos and played the organ at St George’s Catholic Church. Edward read the scores in the shop, played violin in local ensembles, taught several instruments and eventually succeeded his father at the organ. He was born in Lower Broadheath in 1857, a Catholic in a predominantly Anglican musical establishment and a tradesman’s son in a profession increasingly organised around London colleges. He remained sensitive to both distinctions throughout his later success. His practical education taught him how a phrase feels under a bow.

At Powick he wrote quadrilles and polkas for an unusual ensemble, learning to give each instrument useful work. The Three Choirs Festival brought larger repertory within reach: Handel, Mendelssohn and contemporary oratorio, alongside orchestral music from the Continent. Visits to London widened that education. Wagner mattered particularly: the chromatic connection between chords, the orchestral recollection of earlier events and the long postponement of a cadence all entered Elgar’s language. His mature scores acquired part of their English character through their subsequent public use.
